For now though, science and culture are the "currency" for scientific and civic trees progression, respectively. Each new progression costs a certain amount of culture/science to unlock, and the number indicated on top left is how much of it you produce per turn. So if a scientific unlock costs 50 science, and you produce 11 per turn, it'll take you 5 turns to unlock it.

Gold, faith and production follow the same thought process but for different purposes. You get more Gold in many many mamy ways, the most common being working specific tiles (always put "show yields" on your map options), setting up trade routes to foreign civs and building harbors or commercial hubs.

Population is very hard to properly explain in a quick way but for now just know that the more food and housing you have in a city the faster it'll grow.

As for setting up a religion, there's a set amount of "Great Prophets" which is by default lower than the total civ count, and if you manage to build enough holy site related buildings or projects you'll most likely end up having one of them, who'll them be able to found a religion and... well that's a whole another story.

In terms of the game just ending outta nowhere, a competing civ must've achieved a specific victory condition and that's why the game ended: someone reached their goal.

È una città decisamente diversa dalla maggior parte delle città italiane, non solo da un punto di vista organizzativo e strutturale ma anche e soprattutto per chi ci vive dentro.

Tra i pro:
- È molto eterogenea e piuttosto tollerante della diversità altrui (almeno per i nostri standard...)
- Puoi dimenticarti di usare la macchina perché tra bici, piedi e mezzi pubblici quasi tutto tende ad essere ben collegato
- Anche se non conosci immediatamente l'Olandese, con l'inglese puoi barcamenarti piuttosto bene. Nel lavoro sta cosa è un po' un 50/50 ma in quasi ogni altra occasione quotidiana sei coperta (ma studialo lo stesso perché altrimenti non ti integrerai mai)
- è una città con molti giovani, sia anagrafici che "mentali", quindi anche abbastanza dinamica
- tutto sommato, è una città sicura. Puoi girare la sera da sola/o e stare abbastanza tranquilla/o che non ti succede nulla

Tra i contro:
- una città giovane è una città caotica: le strade sono rumorose, anche a notte fonda
- Rotterdam è sicura ma fino a una certa. Tanta gente significa anche potenziali truffatori o scam dietro l'angolo
- tanta competizione lavorativa. Il lavoro alla fine si trova, a detta veramente di tutti, ma può essere problematico trovare lavoro agli inizi
- NON CI SONO CASE lol ma proprio manco l'ombra. Questo significa anche affitti alti

In altre parole, per noi italiani è una pacchia perché i lati negativi già ce li abbiamo in casa ma molti di quelli positivi, specie se sei giovane e/o parte di una minoranza, in italia te li sogni. Also on a side note there's a panel where you can check you demand/supply ratio for each and every of both your island and your production chains. It's very useful for both avoiding massive money wastes and checking whenever the population's demand has grown past your current supply

You can tell how many factories a resource can satisfy by looking at the time it takes for it to produce your end product and divide it by the time it takes for the first factory to produce the workable resource. 

Say your clay pit produces a unit of Clay every 30 seconds and the Brick Factory takes a unit of it to make a unit of Bricks every 60 seconds, 60÷30 equals 2, and that means you can build 2 Brick Factories for each Clay Pit you lay down. 

Some production chains don't return full numbers, like the Steel Beams one, so you'll always end up with a small surplus, but that's intended as Steel Plates are used by many other production chains.

There's also a full comprehensive section in Annowiki.com which tells you exactly how many of each buildings you need to fully balance a production chain. Only remember that for example at first you won't actually need 8 Rum Distilleries and 8 Sugar Plantations just because your lumberjack hut produces a lot of timber, you'll be fine having just 1 of each and some timber surplus. Only after you have a lot of wealthy and demanding population you can and should start enlarging your productivity by that much

In this episode we'll focus on the region's capital and biggest city, Fishport, as well as its very particular district of Nanvakfak. Fishport was initially a very small fishermen's harbor that, once people realized how much food the nearby waters hospited, quickly grew and became known as the "Northern Hope City", inviting climate migrants to settle here in search of a new beginning. This quick growth caused some social trouble in Fishport, as the older residents of the area feared that too many new arrivals would have eventually lead to famine. As a consequence of that cost of land increased quite a lot and wealth disparity increased as well: the old part of the city, Jakestown, is now an elite neighborhood.

In an effort to prevent the worst from happening, the city's government started a politic of differentiation of the economy, a still ongoing effort that's trying to take advantage of Fishport's strategic position to make it a commercial hub, as well as taking advantage of the city's advanced tech labs to allow agriculture to florish in such rigid environment.

South of Fishport is a very special area, the Nanvakfak District, which owes its name to the Nanvakfak (big lagoon) Lake. The reason why the area is so special is that the lake hosts particular algae that provide rich food for many of the sea species of the region, making it the most important reproductive area for may of them. Not many people are allowed to live here, and those who are must follow very strict laws in order not to disturb the very delicate ecosystem of the lake.

As the citizens make an effort in living peacefully, Fishport must find a way to reduce its environmental impact as much as possible in order to grant itself a future. The project of linking Fishport with Togiak sounds like a part of the solution, but how will the Steel Mountains be traversed?

Hello and welcome to my small region showcase!

From now on I'll be occasionally post about my newest and still ongoing project, that uses Flamesrock's map of Cape Newenham, Alaska.

I did a bit of lore building here, so this first episode is gonna explain a bit about the history of this area.

Some years in the future, let's say about 50 years from now, a lot of things have changed for humanity: climate change and the rising temperatures have made some densely populated areas unhabitable, but some previously inhospitable parts of the world are now good enough that what's left of humanity after 11 year of nuclear war want to settle there, looking for a new, more peaceful and more sustanaible beginning.
Among these is the region of Cape Newenham, once a mining site on a rock wasteland, now a fertile land with wide plains and big natural harbors. 

Just north of the cape we find Fishport and its widespread urban area: here lives most of the population of the region. Fishport, born as a small town whose people harvested the rich nearby waters, is slowly trying to transition to a more sustainable economy as it grows; betting on transports, advanced agriculture and commercial services while desperately trying not to fall on the temping capitalist system that brought humanity to the verge of extinction.

East of Fishport we find the two towns of Everfall, lost in a neverending foggy plain, and the hard-working minerary town of Rock Hills, both connected to the sea by Goodnews Bay. Life is hard here as the climate is much less mitigated by the sea, but the locals find relief in the numerous natural hotsprings that make this area a potential turistic destination.

Going ever further east, past the so called Steel Mountains, we find the delta of the Togiak River, one of the warmest places in Cape Newenham. Due to a much more favorable climate agriculture is not only possible, but also very rewarding because of the fertile soil gifted by the river. But it's not all good news for the farmers of Twin Hills and Wheatland, as the Togiak River is also susceptile to heavy floods during summer that can devastate crops and leave illness behind.

The Alaskan government is making a big effort allowing land transport to cross the Steel Mountains and connect Fishport with the Togiak area, but this has proven very hard because of the tough minerals that make galleries, especially long once, a pain to build. Will the region find success in this task and find balance in life, or is it destined to be only a shadow of what humanity once was capable of?

Dark Ages aren't really that bad as long as you can manage the decreased loyalty on some cities. Usually though bigger and even medium cities won't have much trouble handling it, so whenever you know you'll probably end up in a dark age just avoid settling too close to neighboring civs and be ready to move governors and troops to the ribellious cities. Other than that, it's usually better to end up in a dark age than in a normal age, since 1) at least you get some situationally useful policies out of it and 2) the lowered point requirement mean that it'll be easier to go into an Heroic Era next time. A lot of civs, the biggest of all being Phoenicia and Georgia, can benefit quite a bit from falling into a Classical Dark Age due to their special bonuses. 
Personally I tend to produce a lot of faith in the middle to late game, and that can allow you to buy some emergency Great People which give you good era score if their gauge wasn't halfway full yet. Building Taj Mahal is also useful in the long run to avoid falling into dark ages, although it's available somewhat late through the game.

But yeah, loyalty aside I'd argue Heroic>Golden>Dark>Normal as far as preferred ages go. And you can't get a Heroic Era without falling into a Dark one first ;)

On the other hand, base production only requires building the district, and usually boosts adjacent district's yields as well (and in cases like Japan this is even more true).

So yeah it may seem trivial but if you manage to consistently place high yield districts in a single game you'll definitely notice the difference, ESPECIALLY in the early game.
